newsitem.title: USA: Historic tobacco deal could be announced Friday.
newsitem.headline: Historic tobacco deal could be announced Friday.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

The tobacco industry, which once vowed it would never settle lawsuits over smoking, is on the verge of reaching a deal in which it could pay as much as $370 billion to do just that and more, source close to the talks said Thursday.
In what would be an historic agreement, the tobacco companies would settle hundreds of lawsuits, launch major new anti-smoking programs and sharply curtail cigarette advertising.

"We have made tremendous progress ... We got more concessions from the industry today. We hit three triples and scored a few runs. We are very optimistic we can resolve this matter very, very soon," Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, the key state negotiator, told reporters.
Sources involved in the talks being held at a Washington hotel said they expected a deal would probably be announced on Friday.

Although Moore would not reveal details of the talks, the sources said the parties are discussing a fund of as much as $370 billion to be paid out over 25 years. The money would be used for health programs, to settle state suits and certain class actions and to pay for damages in individual cases.

The sources said that under the proposal, punitive damages would not be allowed for individual cases alleging past wrongful behavior. These damages, however, which are awarded to punish and deter wrongful behavior, would be allowed if cigarette companies engage in future wrongdoing.
Part of the package, about $50 billion, is being proposed to specifically "punish" the industry and the amount would be used to pay for health coverage for uninsured children, sources said.

Moore said the nation's top legal officers and industry officials had met continuously since early morning and would continue their talks into late Thursday night. He said discussions would continue on Friday.

He said he had briefed the White House on the status of the talks Thursday and that the meeting was positive. President Bill Clinton is monitoring the negotiations because he and Congress would have to approve any deal before it could be implemented.

Clinton left Washington on Thursday for a summit of world leaders in Denver without his top adviser on the tobacco negotiations, Bruce Lindsey, who stayed behind to monitor the talks. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Lindsey would delay his departure for Denver until Saturday.

Talks between tobacco industry representatives and the state attorneys general have been going on since early April. The negotiations are aimed at a broad settlement of the huge legal claims against the industry in return for increased regulation, advertising curbs and health care programs.

Forty states have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs of treating sick smokers. The states are demanding that the industry agree to be punished for past actions, that it pay damages for smoking-related injuries and that it agree to allow the Food and Drug Administration to regulate cigarettes as a drug.

The shares of tobacco makers rose as investors anticipated an agreement would soon be reached. Philip Morris Cos. and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. were among the most heavily traded stocks on the Big Board. Philip Morris added $2 to $47.50 and RJR rose $1.375 to $35.875.
The companies will not comment on the talks.

Congressmen and financial advisors warned that any preliminary agreement was a long way from becoming a final deal. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said the Senate could not take up related legislation until at least September or October.
"We are pretty much locked out of anything of that nature probably until September or October," the Mississippi Republican told reporters.
Lott and House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, have both expressed doubts in recent weeks about whether Congress would be able to enact tobacco legislation this session.
Mary Aaronson, a Washington advisor to the institutional investment community, also warned that winning Congressional approval could prove difficult.
"Ringling Brothers has nothing on what's about to happen," she said, referring to the famous circus.

The states want to wind up the talks this week. If there is no agreement, Moore has said he will go ahead with presenting Mississippi's case against the industry at the first trial of a state suit set for July 7.
